title: 1 Neurotology
text:
1 Neurotology
THE DIZZY PATIENT
Patients use the term dizziness to describe a wide variety of symptoms: vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, nausea, diplopia, etc. Take the best history you can, but be at peace with the fact that most patients just can’t reliably tell you what they’re feeling (“I don’t know, doc, I just felt off”). Try to sort the rest out with a good neuro exam and the special maneuvers below. If all else fails, all dizzy people over the age of 60, especially with vascular risk factors, should be fully evaluated for an acute neurovascular event.
Your task in the ED is to categorize the patient into one of three groups: 1) Benign Peripheral Positional Vertigo: History: lasts for less than 2 minutes, brought on by head movement
Exam: Dix-Hallpike may produce classic mixed upbeating and torsional nystagmus towards the affected ear that starts
after a delay (10-40 seconds - this takes patience during the exam!), then goes away after 30 seconds (“fatigues”), then the patient may feel spinning in the opposite direction upon sitting up; one side is usually much worse than the other. The response is less severe if you Dix-Hallpike them again (“fatigues”).
Plan: Teach them the Epley, have them follow up with ENT if it doesn’t improve. If it really seems like BPPV without
vertigo/nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike, teach them Epleys anyways; the otolith could also be in the horizontal canal, in which case the test and treatment are different 2) Vestibular system dysfunction (vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis): History: lasts for hours to days; labyrinthitis has hearing loss or tinnitus, vestibular neuronitis does not
Exam: Nystagmus is mixed horizontal-torsional away from the affected side. Head thrust (see vestibulocular reflex
below) – vestibular system dysfunction pt breaks fixation
Plan: Fluids, meclizine, steroid taper. May need admission (to medicine preferably) because they will likely continue
to vomit for several more days 3) Central vertigo: History: lasts hours to days, usually has associated symptoms (eg- dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia, weakness, etc)
Exam: Central Nystagmus: Direction changing (eg. to right in right gaze, left in left-gaze), horizontal/rotatory,
pendular, or vertical. There may be other brainstem or cerebellar findings on exam, but the absence of other symptoms cannot exclude a central cause. Use HINTS to INFARCT (sens 100%, spec 96%; Stroke 2009;40:3504) Tests (mnemonic: HINTS) (note, patient must be currently symptomatic for tests to be reliable) 1. Head Impulse – ask the patient to fixate on your nose and move his/her head rapidly 30o off midline and back to center. Look for corrective saccades. Test is normal in central vertigo, abnormal with peripheral vertigo (vestibular nerve dysfunction). 2. Nystagmus - evaluate in primary gaze and horizontal/vertical gaze in all directions. Benign etiologies have unidirectional nystagmus throughout, although the intensity may be different. Central lesions have horizontal direction change (eg left-beating in left gaze, right-beating in right gaze). Vertical nystagmus is always central. 3. Test of Skew – ask the patient to fixate on your nose and then cover/uncover each eye. If positive, you will see vertical corrective saccade/refixation when moving from one eye to the other (horizontal movement doesn’t count) Test interpretation (mnemonic: INFARCT). Concern for stroke if one or more of the following is true: - Impulse Normal - Fast-phase nystagmus Alternating - Refixation on Cover Test
Plan: Admit as a presumed posterior circulation stroke. PICA infarctions can be subtle and can evolve over time. Be
careful with use of MRI to identify these patients (especially in the ED) – hyperacute MRI may appear falsely negative in posterior fossa infarction

title: 1 Neuro-ophthalmologic Emergencies
text:
1 Neuro-ophthalmologic Emergencies
Acute Third Nerve Palsy - Start with a HCT to rule out subarachnoid blood or herniation. - Complete or partial ophthalmoparesis with pupil involvement requires some type of angiography to evaluate for a compressive aneurysm – start with CTA or MRA but then may still need conventional angiogram. You may also want to get MRI instead of/ in addition to CT scan depending on luxuries of time and resource. - Complete opthalmoparesis with spared pupil in patients over 50 with vascular risk factors is likely ischemic palsy, consider getting an MRI scan and then observing. Usually improve within 2-3 months. - Partial opthalmoparesis with spared pupil could be caused by an aneurysm, angiography is needed. - If in doubt with an acute 3rd nerve palsy, image and obtain angiography.
Pituitary Apoplexy Symptoms: Classic syndrome: HA, sudden visual loss (both visual field and acuity), and ophthalmoplegia). May be accompanied by meningeal signs, hypopituitarism, unstable BP, encephalopathy, facial pain/numbness. Differential: Pituitary tumor infarction or hemorrhage and post-partum hemorrhage/Sheehan syndome. Management: CT scan may miss so MRI (pituitary-protocol) is needed. LP may demonstrate subarachnoid blood and aseptic meningitis. If MRI isn’t conclusive and there is SAH, you may have to get angiographic study to rule out aneurysm. Immediate therapy includes. steroids/hydrocortisone to prevent shock from acute hypopituitarism. Electrolyte abnormalities may be prominent and need to be addressed acutely.
Giant Cell Arteritis Symptoms : HA, tenderness of scalp, temple or face of affected side(s), jaw claudication and current or past history of polymyalgia rheumatic, acute vision loss - anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION), can also have central retinal artery occlusion, posterior circulation infarction. Usually female (ratio 3:1) and over 60-70 (almost unheard of <50 yrs), may have premonitory symptoms of transient monocular blindness, bright light amaurosis, transient binocular diplopia and formed visual hallucinations. Exam: Look for scalp tenderness, visual acuity loss, chalky white disc edema, and cotton wool spots. If evidence of both central retinal artery occlusion and AION, you have likely sealed the diagnosis. Can have motility defects from ischemia of the extra-ocular muscles, nerves or a brainstem infarct Management – Check ESR - most will be above 40 mm/hr in giant cell arteritis. Consult vascular/ophtho for biopsy. Immediately treat with steroids - IV Solumedrol 1 g daily x 3-5 days then 1mg/kg per day PO prednisone. ***Do not wait for biopsy to start treatment!
Ocular Cranial Nerve Palsies: General rules for localization:

Diplopia resolves upon covering one eye: if it doesn’t the problem is likely ocular or refractive.
On cover- uncover testing, an eye that is deviated out (exotropic) will move in when uncovered to pick up the fixation target (usually a finger or your nose)  Think INO, IIIrd n. palsy or exotropia related to medication effect. If the eyes move out with uncover (esotropia)  think of a sixth nerve palsy or abduction deficit.
Mimics of extraocular nerve palsies: thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, decompensated phoria, orbital wall fractures, Wernicke’s syndrome, skew deviation, botulism, orbital tumors, Miller Fisher variant of Guillian-Barre Syndrome, mitochondrial d/o (CPEO: chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, Kearns-Sayre Syndrome), vitamin E deficiency

Afferent visual complaints: 1. History: monocular vs. binocular, pain, timing 2. Exam: acuity (best corrected with glasses and pinhole), color (especially red), visual fields (including blind spot), fundus, pupils (is there an APD) 3. Special tests: visual fields (Humphrey, Goldmann), OCT (quantifies retinal nerve fiber layer thickness), orbital ultrasound and the rest of the neurology favorites (MRI, LP etc.)

title: 1 NIHSS and Tools
text:
1 NIHSS and Tools
rTPA Cryoprecipitate 0.1 units/kg iv if fibrinogen <200 mg/dL
If bleeding is refractory or life threatening consider Aminocaproic acid 4-6 gm IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion 1g/hr for 8 h Enteric- Coated Aspirin
Best supportive care (based on PATCH trial) or 1 unit single donor platelet if a surgical procedure is scheduled or bleeding is refractory (*d/w stroke attg)
Can consider repeat 1 single donor unit if PFA- 100 (orderable in EPIC) is not normalized. Consider DDAVP iv or rVIIa** iv if refractory bleeding Clopidogrel (Plavix®)
Best supportive care (based on PATCH trial) or 2 units of single donor platelets if a surgical procedure is scheduled or bleeding is refractory (*d/w stroke attg)
Consider repeating 2 units Q12 hours until the PFA-100 and Verify Now (Plavix inhibition <20% or PRU over 240) assays are normal. Both tests are orderable in EPIC. Consider DDAVP iv or rVIIa** iv if refractory bleeding **Per P&T committee guidelines adult hematology consult required for approval

title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome, Serotonin Syndrome, and Acute Dystonia
text:
1 Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome, Serotonin Syndrome, and Acute Dystonia
NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME (NMS)
Signs and symptoms

Mental status change: agitated delirium, confusion, encephalopathy (82%)
Muscular rigidity: “lead pipe” tremor (up to 92%) à elevated CPK and myoglobinuric acute renal failure
Hyperthermia: >38°C (87%), >40°C** **(40%)
Autonomic instability: tachycardia (88%), labile BP (77%), tachypnea (73%), diaphoresis

Diagnosis
1.* Exclude other etiologies: *acute drug intoxication, metabolic derangements, meningitis, etc.
Treatment

Admit to ICU
Discontinue offending agent** **(e.g. neuroleptics, D2 blocking antiemetics or abrupt w/d levodopa)
Supportive care for Autonomic instability, DVT/PE prophylaxis, *IVFs to prevent **rhabdo*
Symptomatic treatment:


Agitation - Lorazepam 0.5-1mg prn (may also help with rigidity)
Rigidity – Dantrolene 0.25-2mg/kg IV q6-12 hours (max dose 10mg/kg/day; be aware of hepatotoxicity)
Fever – cooling blankets, ice lavage, acetaminophen

SEROTONIN SYNDROME (SS)
Signs and symptoms
1.* **Mental status change*: agitated delirium, restlessness, disorientation
2.* Neuromuscular hyperreactivi**ty*: tremor, rigidity, myoclonus, rigidity, hyperreflexia (+Babinski and clonus)
3.* **Autonomic instability*: dilated pupils, diaphoresis, hypertension, diarrhea, vomiting
Diagnosis
1.* Exclude other etiologies: *acute drug intoxication, metabolic derangements, meningitis, etc.
Treatment

Admit to ICU

2.** **Discontinue offending agent (e.g. SSRIs, MAOIs, buspirone, trazodone, lithium, opiates, etc.)

Supportive care for Autonomic instability, DVT/PE prophylaxis
Symptomatic treatment:

Agitation, Neuromuscular hyperreactivity - Lorazepam 0.5-1mg prn



Cyptoheptadine (only for severe cases)** **12 mg PO, then 2mg q2 hours until clinical response

ACUTE DYSTONIC REACTION
Signs and symptoms

*I**ntermittent or sustained dystonic posturing* due to blockade of D2 receptor (neuroleptics, certain antiemetics)

Diagnosis

Review medication list/MAR for offending agent.
Exclude metabolic derangements (hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia) or other drug toxicity.

Treatment

Discontinue offending agent
Diphenhydramine 25-50mg IV/IM vs Lorazepam 0.5-1mg IV (acute); Diphenhydramine 25mg PO qid (x48hr)
Alternative therapy: Benztropine 2mg IV/IM (acute); Benztropine 1-2mg PO bid (x48hr)

title: 1 Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus
text:
1 Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus
UF NON-CONVULSIVE STATUS EPILEPTICUS PROTOCOL (ADULT)
Immediately:

Order lorazepam STAT
First 5 min give 2mg lorazepam IVP over 2 min
If still seizing, then repeat dose of 1-2 mg to total of 0.1mg/kg
Watch for hypotension and respiratory depression
Order STAT EEG

5-30 min

Order STAT fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg at rate of 150 mg PE/min (slow rate if hypotension occurs) Maximum dose = 2000 mg
Order Free phenytoin level 2 hours after load. Goal free PHT level of 2-3
If level at goal , start maintenance fosphenytoin 5 mg PE/kg in 3 divided doses per day
If level not at goal, redose using calculation: 0.8 x (weight in kg) x (desired
actual level) x10 = mini-load in mg
can round to nearest 250 mg
Monitor for hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias

By 30 min - Call NeuroCCM fellow phone (352-745-1912) for NICU bed - Convert STAT EEG to Long term video EEG monitoring - Call Epilepsy attending and Neurocritical Care team for further management recommendations and discussion - Options: - Valproic acid: Load IV 40mg/kg; Maintenance: 30 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours (max dose 60 mg/kg/day) Avoid use with liver failure - Lacosamide 400mg bolus ; Maintenance dose: 200 mg IV q 12 hours (max dose 600 mg daily) Monitor for PR prolongation - Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg loading dose; Maintenance dose: 1000 mg IV every 12 hours (max dose 12,000 mg daily) - Phenobarbital total loading dose of 20 mg/kg, divided into smaller 5 mg/kg loading doses at a rate of 10 mg per minute, repeated every two hours until total load given (can be given in non-intubated patient but not preferred, reduced risk of hypotension/ respiratory suppression, typical rate for convulsive status in intubated patient is 60 mg per minute) Monitor for respiratory depression, hypotension - If nonconvulsive seizures continue, intubate and load with midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IV bolus, may repeat bolus dose after 5 minutes if seizures not controlled. Start maintenance dose at 0.1 mg/kg/hr, may increase by 0.1 mg/kg/hr every 20-30 minutes until seizures controlled (usual dose 0.2-0.4 mg/kg/hr; max dose 2.9 mg/kg/hr) monitor for hypotension (patient must be intubated) - If still having nonconvulsive seizures: consider pentobarbital coma (MUST be ordered by CCM) in consultation with Epilepsy attending and General Neurology attending with further management to be determined on a case by case basis
Important Practice Points

Make sure ED weighs patient on arrival; this protocol is contingent on WEIGHT BASED DOSING.
Make sure that timing of doses, infusion rate and actual doses are accurate prior to order (see EPIC status epilepticus order set once available)
If fosphenytoin is not available, can use equivalent dose of phenytoin

text:
1 Optic Neuritis and Transverse Myelitis
OPTIC NEURITIS
Epi: usually 20s-40s, 2:1 F:M Presentation: monocular vison loss/scotoma, red desat, painful eye movements (90%), Uhtoff’s Exam: swollen disks in 1/3 only, central vision loss, poor color plates/red hatpin, +APD
Workup + Admission + Treatment: 1) Blood tests, CXR, and LP are not helpful (unless atypical ON); order MRI for prediction of MS 2) Consider formal VF testing (Goldmann or Humphrey). Consider NMO testing since treatment of this condition is different from routine optic neuritis. 3) Admit for IV Solumedrol 1g/d x 3-5 days, expect recovery in 2-3 weeks 4) Plan to start immunomodulatory therapy if MRI with >2 lesions (>3mm diam, perivent or ovoid) to reduce risk of MS: Interferon beta-1a (Avonex) group had 44% less risk of CDMS at 3 years (CHAMPS trial, Jacobs et al, 2000); interferon beta-1a (Rebif) group had 34% probability of conversion to MS at 2 years (compared to 45% of placebo; ETOMs trial, Comi et al, 2001); interferon beta-1b group had 28% probability of conversion to MS at 2 years (compared to 45% of placebo; BENEFIT trial, Kappos et al, 2006)
Evidence for treatment in acute optic neuritis (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial, 1992,1993,1997) - IV steroids - speed vision recovery, no change in acuity vs. placebo at 5 yrs - IV steroids - 50% less develop CDMS at 2 yrs (8% vs 17%), but no difference at 5 years - Oral steroids - increased recurrent ON vs IV/placebo (41% vs 25%) over 5 yrs (don’t treat acute ON with oral steroids)
ACUTE TRANSVERSE MYELITIS 1. Demyelinating: NMOSD: Dx Criteria: Core Clinical Characteristics: Optic neuritis, acute myelitis, Area postrema syndrome, Acute Brainstem syndrome, Acute diencephalic syndrome Additional MRI requirements: for ON: Optic Nerve MRI inflammation >1/2 optic nerve. For myelitis: cord lesion > 3 segments, MRI brain not c/w MS, NMO-IgG positive (sen 58-76%, sp 85-99%) NMOSD with AQP4-IgG: At least 1 core clinical; Positive AQP4-IgG NMOSD with negative AQP-IgG: At least 2 core clinical (at least 1 has to be ON or TM); Dissemination in space; MRI requirements as applicable

Distinguish from MS: long cord lesions, usually nl MRI brain (atypical when they occur), CSF can have cells (PMN), neg CSF OCBs, NMO Abs rare in MS Treatment: Pheresis (acute); Rituximab (prophylaxis) at 375mg/m2 weekly x 4 weeks (Wingerchuk, et al Neurology 2015:85:1-13)

Misc inflammatory: SLE, Sjogren’s, MCTD, Bechet’s, Sarcoidosis
Nutritional: B12, folate, copper, vitamin E

text:
1 Optic Neuritis and Transverse Myelitis
OPTIC NEURITIS
Epi: usually 20s-40s, 2:1 F:M
Presentation: monocular vison loss/scotoma, red desat, painful eye movements (90%), Uhtoff’s
Exam: swollen disks in 1/3 only, central vision loss, poor color plates/red hatpin, +APD
Workup + Admission + Treatment:

Order MRI brain and ORBITS.
Consider MRI of the spine but if no signs and symptoms, it can be done outpatient.
Consider ophthalmology consultation.
Send ON infectious work up (syphilis, bartonella, lyme), order CDS1 (CNS demyelinating panel) in serum (AQP4 and MOG). If it is more atypical with meningitis and TM, can order MAS1 (myelopathy panel) or ENS2 in serum which includes AQP, MOG . GFAP and CRMP5.
Admit for IV Solumedrol 1g/d x 3-5 days can also do oral
If bilateral, and visual acuity worse than 20/200, long segment, consider MOG- AQP4 and can consider concomitant PLEX

ACUTE TRANSVERSE MYELITIS
History is of outmost importance.
If hyperacute within a few hours, after lifting a heavy object, think vascular.
If worsening over hours to days think autoimmune/infectious
If progressive over weeks think Dural AV Fistula, compressive myelopathy, neoplasia
Approach: 1. MRI GAD à R/o Compression (if compression, call a surgeon). Consider MRI brain to look for MS lesions in brain. 2. If > 3 segments that is considered a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis LETM which changes the differential diagnosis (MS is usually short lesion) and includes, infection, NMO/AQP4, MOGAD, sarcoidosis, Dural AV fistula (dAVF).

If so, consider sending MAS1/MAC1 (it contains all the antibodies that cause myelopathies including AQP4 and MOG) or at least the CDS1 panel (AQP4 /MOG), obtain CSF with basic chemistries and OCB/KFLC/MBP
If pleocytosis, check infectious PCR, cytology, AND flow cytometry on top the Mayo panels (MAS1/MAC1 or at least CDS1) and cytokine panel (serum and CSF)- in Sarcoidosis IL-2 R is usually high and IL-6 as well ( this is a better test than serum -and CSF- ACE)
Serologic testing should include: ANA, SSA/B, ANCA, HTLV-1, HIV-1, RPR, B12, folate, Copper, serum cytokine 13 panel, MAS1 (or at least CDS1)
More ancillary testing: Chest CT (sarcoid), Lip Biopsy (Sjogren’s), Brain/Meningeal Biopsy

ALWAYS LOOK AT THE SAGITAL AND AXIAL. MANY TIMES, YOU CAN TELL WHAT TYPE OF DISEASE IT IS BECAUSE OF CERTAIN CHARACTERISTICS AS FOLLOWS:
AQP4: LETM, swollen the whole cord, contrast with a ring appearance.
MOGAD: LETM, at times with the H sign (gray matter), similar to acute flaccid paralysis seen with arbovirus (Japanese encephalitis virus, EEE, WNV) and enterovirus. Lesions disappear with MOGAD
Sarcoidosis: LETM, usually posterior enhancement, sometimes trident sign, sometimes only leptomeningeal enhancement
Paraneoplastic: LETM but a tractopathy
Spinal cord stroke: Owls eyes (anterior cord syndrome). Hyperacute and first MRI may be negative
Dural AV fistula: LETM in the THORACIC spine, progressive course and presence of flow voids ( but sometimes there is no flow voids) if suspicion, needs to get an angiogram.
NMO: AQP4 +. Brain MRI not consistent with MS
Dx Criteria: Core Clinical Characteristics: 1. Optic neuritis, 2. LETM, 3. Area postrema syndrome (intractable vomiting) >> 4. Acute Brainstem syndrome, 5. acute diencephalic syndrome, and/or 6. acute cerebral syndrome
Additional MRI requirements: for ON: Optic Nerve MRI inflammation >1/2 optic nerve, chiasmatic lesion. For myelitis: cord lesion > 3 segments, MRI brain not c/w MS, AQ4 IgG positive (CDS1 panel)
NMOSD with AQP4-IgG: At least 1 core clinical and a Positive AQP4-IgG. Remember Specificity is near 100% so if the patient ahs AQP4 positive, they have the disease. Sensitivity can be 75% since initially it may be false positive. Only 15% of patients have +OCB
Seronegative NMOSD: At least 2 core clinical events (at least 1 has to be ON or LETM); Dissemination in space; MRI requirements as applicable
Treatment: IVMP > PLEX 5-7d > IVIg if refractory concomitantly. While in the hospital after pheresis can consider Rituximab (1000 mg once) vs Inebilizumab (IL-19, now in formulary, needs to fill a form). Also sartralizumab (IL-6), Ravalizumab (C5), and Eculizumab (C5).
MOGAD: Banwell criteria: Brain MRI not consistent with MS

High titer 1:100-1:1000 + 1 core event: Core event (optic neuritis, myelitis, ADEM, cerebral monofocal or polyfocal deficits, brainstem or cerebellar deficits, cerebral cortical encephalitis)
Low positive titer (1:20 or 1:40), negative AQP4, + supporting MRI/clinical features including

bilateral ON, longitudinal nerve involvement, perineuritis, optic disc edema (given anterior predisposition), LETM, H-sign , conus lesion, ADEM, deep grey involvement, ill-defined brainstem, cerebellum, cerebellar peduncle lesion, cortical cerebral encephalitis that can have leptomeningeal enhancement.
Only 15% of patients have +OCB
Treatment: IVMP +/PLEX/IVIG (acute). MOGAD will need prolonged steroid taper.
If recurrent, may warrant starting DMT such as IVIg, CellCept/prednisone, Rituximab, or Tocilizumab.

1 Acute Manifestations of Parkinson Disease
ACUTE PSYCHOSIS IN PARKINSON’S DISEASE
**Diagnosis**

1. *Exclude secondary causes* *including* infection (UTI, PNA,etc), metabolic derangements, medications.

1. Treat secondary cause if one exists.

title: Seizure Consult
text:
If known epilepsy: goal is to determine ASM regimen and compliance, seizure type/frequency and last seizure, epilepsy physician, any recent triggers (see below). Check ASM levels and if low or they are non-compliant, re-load; if not, consider increasing ASM dose. Ask about prior ASMs tried.
If new onset seizures, obtain comprehensive first seizure history:
• RISK FACTORS: history of febrile seizures, family history of seizures, prenatal and perinatal complications, developmental delay, history of head trauma, history of CNS infection, history of CNS mass/malformation, metabolic disorder, stroke (hemorrhagic>ischemic), drug/alcohol use, consanguinity.
• TRIGGERS LOWERING SEIZURE THRESHOLD: Medications, ASM noncompliance, infection, metabolic abnormalities, toxic ingestion, menses, stress, sleep deprivation, EtOH/benzo withdrawal, fever, use of stimulants, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, acute medical/neuro illness.
• CHARACTERISTICS: aura (visual, auditory, olfactory, epigastric rising sensation, psychic (déjà vu, derealization, depersonalization, fear, anxiety), type of seizure (especially how its starts), eyes open or closed, lateral eye or head deviation, length of seizure, associated tongue bite or other injury, incontinence, post-ictal confusion, post-ictal weakness. Start by asking if they can tell when they will have a seizure.
• SUBTLE SEIZURE SIGNS: history of staring, automatisms, waking up incontinent or injured (tongue bite), myoclonic jerks. May or may not discriminate between epileptic vs. other events. History of injury during events.



Focus on mental status, post-ictal paralysis or other focal deficits, subtle signs of ongoing seizures such as abnormal movements, head or eye deviation/version, eyelid twitching, pupillary abnormalities or hippus; tongue bite/other injury, and meningeal signs



ASM levels (only carbamazepine, phenytoin, valproate and phenobarb levels are available acutely, but others can be helpful to establish compliance), non-contrast head CT (new seizures only!), can consider MRI with/without contrast (seizure protocol). Basic labs including electrolytes and CBC, infectious workup (UA, CXR), toxicology screen, LP if concern for meningitis.
SEE ALOGIRTHMS IN DRIVE OR PRINTED IN TEAM ROOM.






Warning



Not Returning to Baseline after a Seizure?
The two most common reasons patients don’t wake up are prolonged post-ictal periods and overly eager benzo administration … But don’t miss anything important:
·    Make sure the patient isn’t still seizing. Look for subtle abnormal limb or eye movement, fluctuating awareness, or complete lack of improvement. Even though convulsive seizures may be controlled, up to 40% of patients in status may continue having subclinical seizures. Consider a stat EEG.
·    Get a head CT if you don’t have one yet.
·    Consider LP if you have any concern for meningitis/encephalitis or SAH not seen on head CT.
·    You may need to admit a patient overnight for prolonged postictal period or benzo intoxication or if there is no clear medical reason for seizure (e.g., EtOH w/d, infection).

If new onset seizures, obtain comprehensive first seizure history:
• RISK FACTORS: history of febrile seizures, family history of seizures, prenatal and perinatal complications, developmental delay, history of head trauma, history of CNS infection, history of CNS mass/malformation, metabolic disorder, stroke (hemorrhagic>ischemic), drug/alcohol use, consanguinity.
• TRIGGERS LOWERING SEIZURE THRESHOLD: Medications, ASM noncompliance, infection, metabolic abnormalities, toxic ingestion, menses, stress, sleep deprivation, EtOH/benzo withdrawal, fever, use of stimulants, hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, acute medical/neuro illness.
• CHARACTERISTICS: aura (visual, auditory, olfactory, epigastric rising sensation, psychic (déjà vu, derealization, depersonalization, fear, anxiety), type of seizure (especially how its starts), eyes open or closed, lateral eye or head deviation, length of seizure, associated tongue bite or other injury, incontinence, post-ictal confusion, post-ictal weakness. Start by asking if they can tell when they will have a seizure.
• SUBTLE SEIZURE SIGNS: history of staring, automatisms, waking up incontinent or injured (tongue bite), myoclonic jerks. May or may not discriminate between epileptic vs. other events. History of injury during events.

title: Seizure Consult
text: Focus on mental status, post-ictal paralysis or other focal deficits, subtle signs of ongoing seizures such as abnormal movements, head or eye deviation/version, eyelid twitching, pupillary abnormalities or hippus; tongue bite/other injury, and meningeal signs

ASM levels (only carbamazepine, phenytoin, valproate and phenobarb levels are available acutely, but others can be helpful to establish compliance), non-contrast head CT (new seizures only!), can consider MRI with/without contrast (seizure protocol). Basic labs including electrolytes and CBC, infectious workup (UA, CXR), toxicology screen, LP if concern for meningitis.
SEE ALOGIRTHMS IN DRIVE OR PRINTED IN TEAM ROOM.






Warning



Not Returning to Baseline after a Seizure?
The two most common reasons patients don’t wake up are prolonged post-ictal periods and overly eager benzo administration … But don’t miss anything important:
·    Make sure the patient isn’t still seizing. Look for subtle abnormal limb or eye movement, fluctuating awareness, or complete lack of improvement. Even though convulsive seizures may be controlled, up to 40% of patients in status may continue having subclinical seizures. Consider a stat EEG.
·    Get a head CT if you don’t have one yet.
·    Consider LP if you have any concern for meningitis/encephalitis or SAH not seen on head CT.
·    You may need to admit a patient overnight for prolonged postictal period or benzo intoxication or if there is no clear medical reason for seizure (e.g., EtOH w/d, infection).

title: TIA Risk Stratification and Stroke Mechanisms
text:
1 TIA Risk Stratification and Stroke Mechanisms
TIAs:
As a general rule of thumb, moderate/high-risk TIA patients should be observed for 24 hours and evaluated expeditiously for high-risk stroke mechanism. If they want to go home, tell them the risk:
The ABCD2 score predicts risk of stroke within 2 days of a TIA (Lancet 369: 282-292, 2007):
Age ≥60 years [1 point]
Blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg [1 point]
Clinical features: unilateral weakness [2 points], speech impairment without weakness [1 point]
Duration ≥60 min [2 points] or 10–59 min [1 point]
Diabetes [1 point]
Score 6–7 = High risk = 8.1% 2-day risk
4–5 = Moderate risk = 4.1%
0–3 = Low risk = 1.0%
Patients with TIA or minor stroke symptoms (non-disabling, NIHSS ≤ 3) can be admitted to the Clinical Decision Unit (CDU) – must be discussed with stroke attending and ED
Stroke mechanisms:
Most common mechanisms of stroke include:

Cardioembolism (~20% ischemic stroke): Atrial fibrillation (most common, esp in older adults), CHF/CM with low EF, LV or LAA thrombus, cardiac tumor (myxoma/fibroelastoma), mechanical valve, endocarditis (infectious or marantic [autoimmune/malignancy]), paradoxical embolism (PFO, pulm AVM)
Large-artery atherosclerosis (~15%) – extracranial or intracranial (affects treatment choice)
Small-vessel disease (~25%) – must be subcortical/brainstem/cerebellum. Small cortical strokes are generally embolic. Lacunar strokes are usually linked to uncontrolled vascular risk factors.
Rare causes (<5%) – see below, also consider hypercoagulable state from undiagnosed malignancy
Cryptogenic stroke (~20-30%) – no cause found despite thorough workup. If embolic-appearing, may be ESUS (embolic stroke of undetermined source), consider long-term Afib monitoring, no role for empiric AC per ESUS trials to date.

Stroke in Young:
In addition to conventional stroke mechanisms, consider the following for patients <60 years old:
Cardiac disease (including congenital, rheumatic valve disease, mitral valve prolapse, patent foramen ovale, endocarditis, atrial myxoma, arrhythmias, cardiac surgery)
Large vessel disease

Premature atherosclerosis – consider radiation vasculopathy in patients with previous head/neck irradiation. Also consider HIV
Dissection (spontaneous or traumatic)
Inherited metabolic diseases (homocystinuria, Fabry’s, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, MELAS syndrome)
Fibromuscular dysplasia
Infection (bacterial, fungal, tuberculosis, syphilis, Lyme)
Vasculitis (collagen vascular diseases — systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren’s syndrome, polyarteritis nodosa; Takayasu’s disease, Wegener’s syndrome, cryoglobulinemia, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, isolated central nervous system angiitis)
Moyamoya disease
Toxic (illicit drugs — cocaine, heroin, phencyclidine; therapeutic drugs — L-asparaginase, cytosine arabinoside)

Small vessel disease

Vasculopathy (infectious, noninfectious, microangiopathy)

Hematologic disease

Sickle-cell disease, leukemia, thrombocytosis, polycythemia vera
Hypercoagulable states (antiphospholipid antibody syndromes, deficiency of antithrombin III or protein S or C, resistance to activated protein C, increased factor VIII, MTHFR)
DIC, TTP
Venous occlusion (dehydration, parameningeal infection, meningitis, neoplasm, polycythemia, leukemia, inflammatory bowel disease)

Central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist

Central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist

Noncardioselective beta blocker

• Bradycardia• Sleep disturbances

Interacts with alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in brain and spinal cord
• 100 to 300 mg every 8 hours by enteral route• Can rapidly titrate up to 3600 or 4800 mg total daily dose
• Preventive• Improves most features
• Mild sedation


Bromocriptine
Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
• 1.25 mg every 12 hours by enteral route• Can titrate up to 40 mg total daily dose
• Preventive• Effect tends to be modest and delayed
• Agitation• Confusion• Dyskinesia• Nausea/emesis• Orthostatic hypotension• Could reduce seizure threshold


Baclofen
GABA-B agonist
• 5 mg every 8 hours by enteral route• Can titrate up to 80 mg total daily dose (intrathecal option available through implanted pump)
• Preventive• Improves hypertonicity and dystonia
• Sedation• Muscle weakness• Risk of withdrawal (mostly with intrathecal administration)


Dantrolene
Ryanodine receptors in myocytes

• Abortive• Improves hypertonicity and dystonia
• Hepatotoxicity (can be severe)• Respiratory depression• Muscle weakness

title: Mechanical Ventilation
text:
Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) = Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
Pressure Support (PS) is the same physiologic concept as BiPAP PS. The second number in BiPAP is PS (e.g., BiPAP 10/5 = BiPAP 10/5 with PS 5). For BiPAP the first number is CPAP (total pressure), the second number is PS above CPAP.
Assist Control (AC) = Assisted mandatory ventilation (AMV). It can either be volume control or pressure control. Must be positive for lung alveoli to be inflated. Alveolar pressure is what we deliver via the vent.
Compliance = change in volume / change in pressure = ΔV / ΔP. For BiPAP it is total pressure above CPAP. Under normal conditions the tethering of pleura to the chest wall vs. the elastic recoil of lung creates negative pleural pressure.





AC (Assist Control)
Vent delivers a breath at a set rate. If the patient initiates a breath, the ventilator will assist and deliver a full breath with a set tidal volume/pressure.
SIMV (Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation)
Vent delivers set tidal volume at set rate. Patient can breathe in between mandatory breaths.
PS / Pressure Support
Patient-triggered. Vent does nothing unless patient initiates breath. Can be used as a weaning strategy in patients who are doing some work of breathing.
SIMV + PS
Combination of SIMV and PS.
Patient Paralyzed Mode
Vent delivers set pressure and volume depends on compliance. Commonly used as vent weaning mode. It is thought of as a comfortable mode for patients with dyssynchrony. Can’t use in paralyzed patients.
(Waveform diagrams described: AC shows square/consistent breaths; SIMV shows mandatory + spontaneous; PS shows patient-initiated variable breaths; Paralyzed shows passive flow.)

title: Mechanical Ventilation
section: 2 Ventilator Settings: FiO2, PEEP, and Minute Ventilation (Respiratory Rate x Tidal Volume)
text:
2 Ventilator Settings: FiO2, PEEP, and Minute Ventilation (Respiratory Rate x Tidal Volume)
FiO2: Initially 100%. Check ABG to ensure O2 sat correlates with PaO2. After this, can adjust FiO2 down to only what patient needs. Goal SpO2 88-92% in most patients (avoid hyperoxia).
PEEP: Keeps alveoli open to improve oxygenation and reduce atelectasis. Higher PEEP for ARDS / stiff lungs. Caution with high PEEP in unilateral or focal disease (e.g., pneumonia without ARDS).
Pressure Support (PS): Helps overcome resistance of tubing/circuit.
Common starting PEEP: 5 cmH2O. Higher PEEP required for ARDS.

title: Mechanical Ventilation
text:
3 Peak and Plateau Pressures

Peak Pressure: Pressure of respiratory system at end-inspiration. Reflects lungs + chest wall compliance + resistance (tubes, secretions).
Plateau Pressure: Pressure required to hold lungs open (measured during inspiratory pause). Reflects lung + chest wall compliance. Goal < 30 cmH2O.

Respiratory Decompensation — Increased Peak Pressure with unchanged Plateau Pressure often indicates increased resistance (e.g., bronchospasm, mucous plug, kinked tube, patient biting tube).

title: Mechanical Ventilation
text:
4 Additional Concepts
ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome): Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW), higher PEEP.
Permissive Hypercapnia: Allow pCO2 to rise (up to 7.25–7.5 pH) if needed to protect lungs.
Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT): Usually on CPAP of 5 or PS 5–8 with low rate.
Weaning: PS weaning or daily SBTs. Consider trach if prolonged intubation.
Refractory Hypoxia: Consider prone positioning, ECMO, inhaled nitric oxide, etc.

title: Post Cardiac Arrest Management
text:
1 Protocol
Determine if the patient is a candidate for therapeutic hypothermia (comatose + VT/VF/PEA/asystole).
A patient may not be a good candidate if any of the following are present:

Following commands or moving appropriately to noxious stimulation (if any uncertainty, would err on the side of cooling)
Refractory hemodynamic instability
Severe coagulopathy or uncontrolled bleeding (e.g., DIC, severe thrombocytopenia/liver failure, vaso-occlusive disease [e.g., Hgb-SS])
Other, more likely, causes for coma
Significant pre-existing neurologic impairment (e.g., baseline mRS ≥ 4)
End-stage terminal illness (e.g., pre-arrest life expectancy < 6 months)

Additional steps:

Obtain a non-contrast CT head to rule out intracranial hemorrhage, which is a contraindication for hypothermia. In patients with a clear cardiac/pulmonary cause of arrest, the head CT should not delay the start of therapeutic hypothermia.
Arrange for STAT long-term EEG as indicated.
Obtain hepatic and renal function testing (CMP) daily, as well as NSE level ×5 days.

title: Stroke Alert
text:
2 Initial Steps

Last known normal (LKN): When was the patient last known normal? Don’t trust anybody — FIND OUT YOURSELF. Obtain family phone contact information from EMS in case needed for timeline confirmation and eventual consent.
Brief medical history: Similar sx in past, acuity of onset, fluctuation/progression of sx, known stroke causes (Afib, carotid disease), associated sx (headache/neck pain, altered consciousness, abnormal movements), current antithrombotics.
Check blood pressure.
Fingerstick glucose. Correct if <50 or >400. If still symptomatic, proceed with acute vascular workup.
Rapid neuro exam/NIHSS — do NOT delay CT/IV/blood draw. Learn to work around ED providers.
Take patient to CT scan as soon as possible.

UF stroke alert protocol: non-contrast HCT, CTA head/neck, and CT perfusion.
Non-contrast HCT alone is sufficient for TNK decision. If perfusion scanner is down, do NOT waste time.
Stay with the patient and immediately review the scan yourself.

Review TNK inclusion/exclusion criteria.
Call stroke attending/fellow as soon as possible.
Review risks/benefits with patient/family. Obtain verbal consent if possible (see suggested language below).
If TNK planned:

Inform nurse/pharmacist/ED team.
Get weight in kilograms.
Place order in Epic: TNK (single bolus) 0.25 mg/kg; max 25 mg (order set: ‘NEURO Stroke Thrombolytic Administration’).
Ensure 2 well-functioning IVs (preferably 20-gauge or larger).
BP must be <185/110 before pushing TNK.
Remain at bedside until TNK administered.

Consider mechanical thrombectomy and/or acute stroke clinical trial.

Suggested consent language:
“You are having an acute stroke, caused by a blood clot blocking one of the arteries in your brain. The symptoms you’re currently having may become permanent if we don’t act quickly. You qualify for a medication called TNK, which will help dissolve the blood clot. Studies in thousands of patients with strokes like yours have shown that with this medication, patients have a much better chance of recovering to normal and living at home after a stroke. Because this medication temporarily thins your blood, there is a possible risk of bleeding, including bleeding in the brain. However, the potential benefit from the treatment is 6–10 times greater than the risks of harm, and I believe this medication is the best chance we have of reversing your symptoms. The faster we start the treatment, the better your chances of recovery. Do we have your permission to proceed?”
If BP elevated:
- Labetalol 10-20 mg IV over 1-2 minutes, may repeat ×1 OR
- Nicardipine gtt at 5 mg/hr IV, titrate by 2.5 mg/hr every 5-15 min (max 15 mg/hr). Consider clevidipine.

2.1 Tenecteplase Inclusion Criteria

Clinical diagnosis of stroke with disabling neurological deficits
Symptom onset / last seen normal within past 4.5 hours

AHA 2026 Absolute & Relative Contraindications

Absolute ContraindicationsRelative ContraindicationsNo Contraindication (Generally Safe)









Condition
Details




CT with extensive hypodensity
IV thrombolysis should not be administered to patients whose brain imaging exhibits regions of clear hypodensity that appear to be responsible for the clinical symptoms of stroke. Clear hypodensity is when the degree of hypodensity is greater than the density of contralateral unaffected white matter.


CT with hemorrhage
IV thrombolysis should not be administered to patients when CT brain imaging reveals an acute intracranial hemorrhage.


Moderate to severe traumatic brain injury <14 days
For patients with AIS and a history of recent moderate to severe traumatic brain injury within 14 days that incurred >30 minutes of unconsciousness and Glasgow Coma Scale of <13 OR evidence of hemorrhage, contusion, or skull fracture on neuroimaging.


Neurosurgery <14 days
For patients with AIS and a history of intracranial/spinal surgery within 14 days, IV thrombolysis is potentially harmful and should not be administered.


Acute spinal cord injury within 3 months
For patients with AIS who harbor an intraspinal/intramedullary neoplasm, treatment with IV thrombolysis is potentially harmful and should not be administered.


Intracranial neoplasm
For patients with AIS who harbor an intracranial neoplasm, treatment with IV thrombolysis is potentially harmful and should not be administered.


Infective endocarditis
For patients with AIS and symptoms consistent with infective endocarditis, treatment with IV thrombolysis should not be administered.


Severe coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia
The safety and efficacy of IV thrombolysis for AIS in patients with platelet count <100,000/mm³, INR >1.7, aPTT >40 s, or PT >15 s is unknown though may substantially increase risk of harm and should not be administered.


Aortic arch dissection
For patients with AIS and known or suspected aortic arch dissection, treatment with IV thrombolysis is potentially harmful and should not be administered.


Amyloid angiopathy / CAA-ri
The risk of thrombolysis-related ICH in patients on amyloid immunotherapy or with ARIA is unknown and IV thrombolysis should be avoided in such patients.












Condition
Details




Pre-existing disability
The benefits and risks of offering IV thrombolysis to patients with pre-existing disability and/or frailty remain uncertain. Treatment should be determined on an individualized basis.


DOAC exposure
For patients taking a direct oral anticoagulant, the safety of IV thrombolysis is uncertain. In the absence of specific laboratory tests (anti-Xa or dilute thrombin time) and time of last dose is unknown or <48 h, benefit/risk discussion is required.


Major surgery or serious trauma within 14 days
For patients with AIS who have undergone major surgery or serious trauma within the previous 14 days, IV thrombolysis may be considered after weighing the risk of surgical-site bleeding versus the anticipated benefit of thrombolysis.


GI or GU hemorrhage within 21 days
For patients with AIS who have a history of previous GI or GU hemorrhage within 21 days, IV thrombolysis may be considered after weighing the risk of recurrent hemorrhage versus the anticipated benefit of thrombolysis.


Recent major surgery
For patients with recent major surgery (within 14 days) or serious trauma, treatment with IV thrombolysis may be considered after weighing the risk of surgical-site hemorrhage versus the anticipated benefits of thrombolysis.


Prior ICH
For patients with a history of previous ICH, IV thrombolysis may be considered after weighing the risk of recurrent ICH versus the anticipated benefit of thrombolysis.


Recent myocardial infarction
For patients with recent MI (within 3 months), treatment with IV thrombolysis may be considered after weighing the risk of myocardial rupture versus the anticipated benefits of thrombolysis.


Seizure at onset
For patients with AIS presenting with seizure at onset who have residual post-ictal deficits, IV thrombolysis may be considered if residual deficits are thought to be due to stroke rather than a post-ictal state.


Blood glucose <50 or >400 mg/dL
For patients with AIS and blood glucose <50 mg/dL or >400 mg/dL, IV thrombolysis may be considered after glucose is corrected and residual deficits persist.


Pregnancy
For patients with AIS who are pregnant, IV thrombolysis may be considered after careful weighing of maternal and fetal risks versus benefits.


Arterial puncture at noncompressible site within 7 days
For patients with AIS who have had an arterial puncture at a noncompressible site within the previous 7 days, IV thrombolysis may be considered after weighing the risk of access-site hemorrhage versus the anticipated benefits of thrombolysis.


Large untreated aneurysm
For patients with AIS and a large untreated intracranial aneurysm, the safety of IV thrombolysis is uncertain.












Condition
Details




Menstruation
IV thrombolysis is unlikely to be associated with clinically significant menstrual bleeding and is reasonable in otherwise eligible patients.


Extracranial cervical artery dissection
IV thrombolysis in patients with AIS and extracranial cervical artery dissection is likely low risk and is reasonable.


Unruptured intracranial aneurysm
IV thrombolysis in patients with AIS and unruptured intracranial aneurysm is likely low risk. Benefit likely outweighs risk.


Angiography
IV thrombolysis in patients with AIS during or immediately after angiography is reasonable.


Microbleeds
The risk of symptomatic ICH in patients with AIS and small numbers of cerebral microbleeds is low. IV thrombolysis is reasonable.


GI bleeding remote
For patients with remote history of GI bleeding who are otherwise candidates for IV thrombolysis, treatment is reasonable.


History of stroke
Patients with history of previous ischemic stroke who are otherwise candidates may still receive IV thrombolysis after individual risk-benefit discussion.


Moyamoya
IV thrombolysis in patients with Moyamoya disease does not appear to pose a substantial increased risk.

3 Mechanical Thrombectomy
Consideration should begin immediately after TNK decision.
General eligibility: Large-vessel occlusion on CTA (M1, M2, A1, P1, ICA, basilar), symptom onset <24h, NIHSS ≥6, ASPECTS ≥3.

Symptom onset <6h: Do NOT wait for CTP per AHA.
6-24h: Ideal = large penumbra/small core on CTP (DAWN/DEFUSE-3); benefit even with large core (ASPECTS ≥3).
Hyperacute MRI/MRA if contrast issue (discuss with neurorads).


Review LVO <24h LKW with stroke fellow/attending.
Stroke attending calls endovascular neurosurgery.

Place admission orders ASAP.

(use order set “NEURO Stroke POST Thrombolytic Administration”)

Admit to NICU (call CCM fellow)
BP monitoring: maintain <180/105

Vitals q15 min ×2h, then q30 min ×6h, then q1h ×16h

No heparin, warfarin, aspirin, or other antithrombotics for 24h if TNK given
Avoid invasive procedures (NG, Foley, non-compressible arterial access) for 24h if TNK
Repeat CT head 24h post-TNK — if negative, start ASA 325 mg and DVT prophylaxis

title: Stroke Alert
text:
5 Complications of TNK
Intracranial hemorrhage and angioedema

5.1 Angioedema

Assess airway immediately
Epinephrine 0.5 mL IM + Benadryl 25 mg IV



5.2 Suspected Intracranial Hemorrhage

Worsening LOC, new/worsening neuro deficits, nausea/vomiting, severe headache, Cushing response, seizure
STAT CT head
CALL ATTENDING/FELLOW IMMEDIATELY
Labs: CBC, PT/PTT, platelets, fibrinogen, D-dimer
Tighten BP: SBP 100-140 (nicardipine infusion)
Reversal: Cryoprecipitate 10 units IV + TXA 1 g IV (if indicated)
Obtain TEG/fibrinogen 2h post-reversal; repeat cryo if fibrinogen <150
Refractory/life-threatening bleed: consider aminocaproic acid

Always discuss management with stroke attending/fellow.

3 Control BP: Goal SBP 100–140

Use labetalol 10–20 mg IVP q1h PRN or nicardipine drip (start at 5 mg/h and titrate up as needed). If a nicardipine drip is started, ask ED resident/attending to place arterial line. A PIV can only be used for 24 h.

text:
4 Additional guidelines and workup

ABCs, intubation if GCS <8
HOB > 30°
